## A 30-Day Plan to Build a Product Team That Learns Faster


Contributors:


No items found.


AI has made building cheap, and that's good news for product leaders. Your team can now spend far more of its time deciding what deserves to be built.


We'd bet the teams that pull ahead over the next year will be the ones that learn from customers fastest. You can start building that this quarter.


### Judgment is now your team's biggest lever


Marty Cagan, founder of Silicon Valley Product Group and former SVP of product and design at eBay, put it simply this spring:[the real bottleneck is in discovering a solution that's worth building](https://www.svpg.com/build-to-learn-vs-build-to-earn/) . Oji Udezue, who has led product at Typeform, Calendly and Atlassian, made a related point:["Every product practice you go through is constructed around the bottleneck resource of engineering."](https://www.mindtheproduct.com/oji-udezue-at-industry-leadership-forum-2025-why-your-ceo-will-ship-faster-than-you/)


Most of your rituals were designed to ration engineering time. That means you get to redesign them around something that matters more: making better calls, faster.


Julie Zhuo, who rose to VP of design at Facebook and wrote The Making of a Manager, expects the bulk of future product development[will be spent researching whether an idea has legs](https://lg.substack.com/p/the-death-of-product-development) . For most PMs, that's the best part of the job. It's the work they got into product to do.


### What fast-learning teams do differently


**Customer conversations are part of the weekly rhythm.** PMs keep a few customer conversations on the calendar every week, the same way they keep a standup. When a big question comes up, there's already someone to ask.


**Prototypes reach customers before roadmaps get locked.** Prototypes are cheap now, so strong teams put a rough version in front of five customers before committing a quarter to it. Five conversations cost a lot less than a sprint spent on the wrong thing.


**The circle of voices keeps widening.** These teams check who they've been hearing from and go find the segments they haven't. It keeps the roadmap pointed at the market they want to win.


**The right way is also the easy way.** Researchers set the standard for how the team reaches customers, and the tooling takes care of scheduling and admin. That way more of your team can talk to customers without anyone becoming a part-time scheduler.


### A 30-day plan to get started


Pick one roadmap bet your team plans to commit to next quarter and run it through this.


1. **Week 1: Name the riskiest assumptions.** Use the first prompt below to list what has to be true for the bet to work, ranked by risk.
2. **Week 2: Get in front of five customers.** The PM talks to five target customers, with a rough prototype if you have one. The second prompt helps them prep.
3. **Week 3: Review the evidence together.** Bring the top assumption to your leadership meeting with a clear verdict: confirmed, disproved or still open.
4. **Week 4: Make the call and measure it.** Commit, cut or reshape the bet. Note how many days it took to get from idea to real customer evidence. That number is your baseline.


Next month, run it again with a different bet. By the third round, nobody needs to put it on the agenda.


### Three prompts to help you run it


These work in Claude with the docs, notes and exports you already have.


Find the riskiest assumptions in a roadmap bet


Here is a roadmap item we plan to commit to next quarter, along with the customer evidence behind it \[insert notes, quotes, tickets, data\]. List the assumptions that have to be true for this to succeed. Rank them by how risky they are and how little evidence we have. For the top three, suggest the fastest way to test each with five target customers.


Prep for five customer conversations


I'm a product manager testing this assumption: \[assumption\]. This week I'm talking to five target customers for 30 minutes each, and I may show a rough prototype. Write a short conversation guide: how to open, five open questions about their recent real experience with this problem, what to watch for when they see the prototype, and any leading questions to avoid.


Measure how fast your team learns


Here is a list of our last ten significant product decisions with the date each was proposed and the date it was committed, plus a log of customer conversations over the same period. For each decision, estimate when we first spoke to customers about it, how many we spoke to, and how many days passed between the idea and real customer evidence. Summarize where we learn fastest and where we could speed up.


### Three numbers to keep an eye on


You'll know it's working when these move in the right direction.


- **Days from idea to customer evidence.** Watch it drop month over month.
- **Share of big bets tested with customers before commit.** Start with any bet bigger than a few weeks of work.
- **Number of distinct accounts and segments behind last quarter's decisions.** The wider the mix, the more your roadmap reflects the market you want to win.


### Start with one bet


This is a good moment to lead a product team. Building keeps getting easier, which leaves more room for the part of the job most product people love: understanding customers well enough to build the right thing. Pick one bet this week and see how fast your team can learn.
